The View from SomewherePart I · The idea

Chapter 1

Local views

Web edition. Figure 1.3 is live: change it and watch the ideas move.

Stand on a hillside in fog with a surveyor’s level and a staff. You can do one thing well. You can tell how much higher the stake over there is than the stake under your boots. You cannot tell how high either stake is above sea level, because nothing in the fog carries that label. Now put a dozen surveyors on the same hill, each in a pool of visibility that holds a handful of stakes, with neighboring pools sharing a stake or two. Each of them goes home with a tidy private map in which every height is measured from her own first stake.

This chapter asks the question the whole book hangs on. When do those private maps fit together into one map of the hill? When they do not, what has gone wrong, and where? The first book called the one map “the hill”, and its rule was that nobody gets to stand on it. Here we take the rule seriously and see what is left to say with only the pools.

The answer comes in three steps, and I will take them slowly because everything later leans on them. First the vocabulary of local data: sections, restriction, overlaps, gluing. Then the observation that decides most cases, which is that pieces arranged in a tree always glue and pieces arranged around a loop may not. Then the definition of a sheaf on a graph, with its two numbers, H0 for what glues and H1 for what stops it. The surveyors, the hill and every number attached to them are invented.

1.1Local data

Figure 1.1 shows an invented hill with two surveyors’ pools on it. Surveyor 1 works inside the left ellipse and levels between the stakes A, B and D. Surveyor 2 works inside the right ellipse, where the stakes are B, D and C. The two ellipses overlap, and B and D are the stakes in the overlap.

Heights in meters, each from the surveyor’s own start A B D C
Surveyor 1, starting at A 0.00 10.81 11.58 –
Surveyor 2, starting at C – 9.52 10.29 0.00

Look at the table before reading on. The two surveyors report different heights for the same stake: B is 10.81 meters above A on the first list and 9.52 above C on the second. Neither is wrong. Each list is a set of heights measured from a start that the surveyor chose, and a list shifted up or down by any constant would serve her just as well, because nothing she can measure inside her pool tells the shifted list from the original. What she actually knows is the differences. The step from B to D is 0.77 meters on both lists, and that is the one thing the two pools can check against each other.

So I will say what “local data” means in this chapter. A pool is a region of the hill, which I will call an open set U when I need to be exact. The data a surveyor holds on her pool is what I will call a section over it: a height for every stake, or more generally a height function, defined on that pool and nowhere else. Over a smaller pool inside hers she can simply forget the stakes outside it, and that forgetting is called restriction. The stakes B and D lie in the overlap of the two pools, so each surveyor can restrict her section to the overlap and the two restrictions can be compared. If they agree there, nobody has contradicted anybody. Whether that is enough for one map of the hill to exist is the question of gluing.

1.2Restriction and gluing

Here is the definition that the textbooks use, so that you recognize it when you meet it. Let X be a space, here the hillside, and let U, V be open subsets of it, which for us means regions without their boundary curves, so that every point has some elbow room.

A presheaf F assigns to every open set U a collection F(U) of “things of a given kind that make sense on U”, and to every pair V⊆U a restriction map F(U)→F(V), written s↦s|V. Restricting from U to U must change nothing, and restricting from U to V and then to a smaller W must be the same as restricting from U to W at once. That is all a presheaf is. A sheet of sketches of the terrain, cut down with scissors to a smaller patch, is the standard picture.

A presheaf is a sheaf if, whenever an open set U is covered by smaller open sets Ui, two conditions hold:

  1. Locality. If two elements of F(U) have the same restriction to every Ui, they are equal.

  2. Gluing. If you choose an element si∈F(Ui) for each i and they agree on every overlap, si|Ui∩Uj=sj|Ui∩Uj, then some s∈F(U) restricts to every si.

The two together say that a thing on the whole is the same as a compatible family of things on the parts. Read the definition as a detector. It asks of a kind of information whether it is genuinely local, and three small examples show what passing and failing look like.

Continuous functions pass. Let F(U) be the continuous real functions on U. Functions on the pieces that agree on overlaps define one function on the union, and it has no jump because a jump would have to sit at some particular point, and near every point the glued function equals one of the jump-free pieces.

Bounded functions fail. Let F(U) be the bounded real functions on U. Cover the real line by the intervals (n−1,n+1) and take sn(x)=x on each. Every sn is bounded and they agree on overlaps. The only candidate for the glued function is x on the whole line, which has no ceiling. Whether a function stays under a ceiling is a claim about the entire domain at once, and no collection of local checks can establish it.

Constant functions on separate pieces fail. Let F(U) be the functions on U that take one value throughout U. Take U to be two separate islands, and let s1=0 on one island and s2=1 on the other. The overlap is empty, so the two agree on it trivially, and no single-valued function on both islands restricts to both. The smallest repair is to allow functions that are constant on each connected piece of U, which is what mathematicians mean by a locally constant function.

The last example is worth keeping near the surveyors, because the data in Figure 1.1 is not exactly a sheaf of heights. It is closer to a sheaf of slopes. What the ground gives each surveyor, and what both surveyors agree on in the overlap, is how steep it is and in which direction. A height list is one choice of potential for those slopes, and a potential is only fixed up to a constant. Two potentials with the same slopes on an overlap therefore differ there by a locally constant function. When the overlap is in one piece, as it is everywhere in this chapter outside the exercises, that is a single constant, and I will write φj−φi=cijon Ui∩Uj.φj−φi=cijon Ui∩Uj. In the figure, φ1 is surveyor 1’s list, φ2 is surveyor 2’s, and c12=9.52−10.81=−1.29 at B and 10.29−11.58=−1.29 at D: the same number at both stakes, which is what agreement of the slopes means. The constants cij are numbers attached to pairs of overlapping pools. We may shift each local potential by a constant ki of our choice, replacing φi by φi−ki, and that changes cij to cij−(kj−ki). The local potentials fit into a single height function on the whole hill exactly when we can choose the ki to make every cij vanish: cij=kj−kifor some choice of k1,k2,….cij=kj−kifor some choice of k1,k2,…. In Figure 1.1 that is easy. Raise surveyor 2’s list by 1.29 meters and it agrees with surveyor 1’s at both shared stakes, and the glued map says C stands 1.29 meters above A. With two pools there is one number c12 and one shift k2−k1 to absorb it. The trouble starts when there are more pools than that.

1.3Trees and loops

Draw a point for each pool and join two points when the pools overlap. Figure 1.2 shows what that graph looks like for two arrangements of pools. In the first the pools form a chain, each overlapping the next. In the second there are five pools arranged around a lake, so that the last meets the first.

On the chain, gluing always works, and the reason is short enough to give in full. Leave U1 alone: k1=0. The overlap with U2 gives c12=k2−k1, which tells us k2. The overlap with U3 then tells us k3, and so on down the chain. Each pool is reached by exactly one route from the first, so exactly one equation determines its shift, and nothing remains that could contradict it. The same argument works on any tree: pick a root, walk outward, and every node has one way in.

On the ring, walk the same way and arrive at U5 with a value of k5. But U5 also overlaps U1, and that overlap makes its own demand, c51=k1−k5. The two demands agree exactly when c12+c23+c34+c45+c51=0, the sum of the offsets once around the lake. Every pair of neighboring pools may agree perfectly on its overlap, and the five together may still fail to describe one map, because the closing overlap supplies a second route to a pool that was already placed. This is the sentence to put on a card if the book had only one: local views on a tree always glue, and a loop is the only place gluing can fail.

The sentence needs care, because on a real hill the loop does close. If the offsets all come from one height function, their sum around the ring is zero because the heights cancel in pairs. A ring fails to close for one of three reasons. The surveyors may have made mistakes, which is the case the next section works. The thing surveyed may have a hole in it, so that slopes that look like a gradient near every point are not the gradient of anything on the whole, as with the angle measured around a circle: near any point it is a good function, and after one lap it has gone up by a full turn. Or the surveyors may not measure the same thing in the same way, so that the shifts ki become translations that need not compose, which is Chapter 4. When the region has no hole, loops of pools can be shrunk to nothing by triple overlaps, and genuine slopes give a zero sum. The lake is what makes the ring a loop that cannot be shrunk.

1.4A staircase that closes on itself

Take four stations on a ring: A, B, C and D, and let each pair of neighbors report a height difference. Figure 1.3 shows two sets of reports, an invented one that is consistent and one that is not.

Each report is a plain step, and a single report is not wrong in any way you could point to. What goes wrong is the walk. On the right of the figure you climb 0.30, climb 0.20, descend 0.35, descend 0.05, and end the lap 0.10 meters higher than you began, at the station you began at. That is the Penrose staircase, the one Escher used for his monks, in arithmetic. Cover any corner of the staircase with your hand and what is left is an ordinary stair. The impossibility is not located anywhere. It exists only for the walker who goes all the way round.

Surveyors call the leftover the misclosure. Kirchhoff’s voltage law is the same statement about a circuit, with voltages for heights: a closed loop in which the voltage changes do not sum to zero would run forever for nothing. The logic is a pair of sentences, and the second is the one that matters. If there are true heights underneath, every loop of reports sums to zero. Read backwards: a loop that does not sum to zero proves that no heights exist, and it proves it from the reports alone, without anyone climbing the hill to look.

What the loop sum does not do is say which report is at fault. On the right of Figure 1.3 any one of the four reports, or several, may be the culprit, and a single ring treats its four steps symmetrically. That limit returns in Chapter 3.

How wrong?

When the reports do not close, there is still a best map. Gauss’s answer, which Chapter 3 builds properly, is to move every report as little as possible, in the least-squares sense, until the walk closes. On a ring of n stations the answer is easy to see. Spread the misclosure evenly: each of the four reports in the inconsistent panel moves by −0.10/4=−0.025, and the adjusted reports are 0.275, 0.175, −0.375 and −0.075. They sum to zero. Heights measured from A become 0, 0.275, 0.450 and 0.075 for A,B,C,D. The size of the compromise is the misclosure divided by n, here 0.10/2=0.05 in the root-sum-of-squares of the adjustments. Figure 1.3 does these computations for any reports on its ring of four stations.

1.5A sheaf on a graph

Everything so far was a special case. Surveyors’ pools are the simplest data; in the rest of the book each pool will keep its own variables, and a shared space between two pools will not need to be the same as either. I want the definition that allows that, and on a graph it needs only linear algebra.

Start with the plain-language version. A graph has vertices, which are positions: a person, a town, a survey. Each vertex holds a view, and the views at different vertices need not be of the same kind. A graph also has edges, joining positions that can compare notes. An edge holds the shared vocabulary of its two endpoints, the terms in which they can actually say something to each other. And each end of an edge has a translation, which takes the vertex’s own view and writes it in the edge’s terms. A global section is a choice of one view at every vertex such that, on every edge, the two translations come out equal. In words: no pair of neighbors disagrees once they speak in the terms they share.

Figure 1.4 draws a concrete case, an invented one taken from the first book. Town A tracks the prices of wheat and fish, town B wheat and cloth, town C fish and cloth. Two towns can compare only what both track: A and B wheat, B and C cloth, C and A fish.

Now the precise statement.

Definition. A cellular sheaf F on a graph G=(V,E) has a vector space F(v) for every vertex, called its stalk; a vector space F(e) for every edge; and for every vertex v on an edge e a linear restriction map Fv→e:F(v)→F(e).

Collect the views of all the vertices into one vector, and the shared spaces of all the edges into another: C0=⨁v∈VF(v),C1=⨁e∈EF(e).C0=⨁v∈VF(v),C1=⨁e∈EF(e). A point x∈C0 is a choice of a view xv at every vertex. Fix a direction u→v on each edge. The coboundary δ:C0→C1 measures the disagreement on each edge: (δx)e=Fv→exv−Fu→exu. Then H0(G;F)=ker⁡δ,H1(G;F)=C1/imδ=cokerδ.H0(G;F)=ker⁡δ,H1(G;F)=C1/imδ=cokerδ. An element of ker⁡δ is a global section, a choice of views with no disagreement anywhere. For the three towns, δx=(wB−wA,cC−cB,fA−fC).

One operator, two questions. The kernel asks which choices of views have no disagreement. The image asks which patterns of disagreement can arise from some choice of views, and its cokernel H1 is what the image misses. In the surveying problem this is exactly the situation of the last two sections. The vertices carry heights, the edges carry height differences, and the reports t∈C1 are a point of the space of possible disagreement patterns. A report comes from heights if and only if t lies in the image of δ, and the obstruction is the class of t in H1.

For the constant sheaf, with every stalk equal to R and every restriction map the identity, which is the mathematical form of “everyone looks at the same thing”, everything can be counted. ker⁡δ is the set of functions constant on each connected piece of the graph, so dim⁡H0 is the number c of connected pieces. For H1, take one spanning tree in each piece. Walking along tree edges from a root fixes a height for every vertex, and a report on tree edges can always be matched. Each of the remaining E−V+c edges closes exactly one loop with the tree, and the report is a coboundary if and only if each of those loop sums is zero. So dim⁡H0=c,dim⁡H1=E−V+c,dim⁡H0=c,dim⁡H1=E−V+c, the number of independent loops. Obstructions live on loops. A tree has none, which is the whole of Section 1.3 in one line.

Table 1.1: Dimensions of H0 and H1, computed as dim⁡C0−rankδ and dim⁡C1−rankδ from the matrices themselves. On every constant-sheaf row they equal c and E−V+c. Generated by figures/ch01_dims.py.
Graph Sheaf dim⁡C0 dim⁡C1 rank δ dim⁡H0 dim⁡H1
Path on four stations constant 4 3 3 1 0
Two separate pairs constant 4 2 2 2 0
Triangle constant 3 3 2 1 1
Square constant 4 4 3 1 1
Square with a diagonal constant 4 5 3 1 2
Three towns, two goods each goods 6 3 3 3 0
The same, plus a wheat-only hamlet goods 7 5 4 3 1

The last two rows of Table 1.1 are the interesting ones. The three towns that track two goods each form a triangle, and the constant sheaf on a triangle has a loop, but here H1=0. δ has rank 3 and C1 has dimension 3, so every pattern of disagreement is attainable. Wheat is discussed only on one side of the triangle, cloth on another, fish on the third. A loop of towns is not a loop of any one good, and it is the goods that have to close up. And H0 has dimension 3: one agreed price for wheat, one for cloth, one for fish. That is a complete three-good price system, and no town has ever tracked three goods. The shared view holds more than any participant’s view; it was assembled from the pieces, and it is consistent. Add a hamlet that tracks wheat only and trades with both A and B (last row) and a loop appears in wheat alone. H0 is still of dimension 3 and H1 has dimension 1.

Figure 1.5 shows what H1 is in the smallest constant case, the triangle with its three reports (tAB,tBC,tCA). They live in R3. Reports that come from heights fill a plane, the image of δ, where the three sum to zero. The quotient C1/imδ is what is left when you identify points that differ by a vector in the plane, and what survives is the loop sum s=tAB+tBC+tCA: the distance from the plane, in a convenient unit. For the report (0.30,0.20,−0.10) the sum is 0.40, and the nearest consistent report is the foot of the perpendicular from the report to the plane, (0.167,0.067,−0.233). That is the least-squares adjustment of the previous section, one third of the misclosure taken from each report.

One more point about the definition, so that you can read the books. The network definition is the space definition of Section 1.2 applied to a small space made from the graph. The basic open sets are a vertex together with all the edges at it, and a single edge on its own; F(v) is the data on the first and F(e) the data on the second, and Fv→e is restriction from the first to the second. So “restriction map” was the right name all along, even though on a graph it looks like translation. The sheaf notes cite Curry’s thesis for this equivalence from memory, and this project never opened the thesis, so we give it as a statement that has not been checked.

1.6What the papers say

What the paper says: Hansen and Ghrist (2021), Opinion dynamics on discourse sheaves

They define the object of the last section, for the purpose of modeling opinions. A vertex stalk is an agent’s private opinion space, an edge stalk is the space in which two agents talk to each other, and a restriction map is how an agent expresses an opinion in that space. Their coboundary measures disagreement of expression, and they stress that agreement of expression on an edge does not mean the two agents hold the same opinion; it means their stated views look the same. The sheaf Laplacian L=δ⊤δ drives a diffusion x˙=−αLx which converges, exponentially at a rate set by the spectrum of L, to the orthogonal projection of the starting opinions onto H0. If the sheaf has no nonzero global sections the only stable opinions are zero. Two further results matter for later chapters. Theorem 9 says that if no nonzero global section vanishes on a set Y of agents, then observing the agents on Y recovers the part of the network’s state that persists, its projection onto H0. That is an identification condition, and the paper states it without proof, as the dual of its Theorem 8 on steering the network. Theorem 11 describes agents who keep their opinions and adjust how they express them, so that the sheaf moves to the nearest one for which the current opinions are consistent. We read all thirteen sections of the arXiv version, theorem statements and examples included, and skipped the proof bodies; we did not compare the journal version. The paper has no preferences, prices or markets, and its own list of open directions includes probabilistic elements, so we would not look in it for a noise model or a test.

What the paper says: Bosca and Ghrist (2026), Selective adaptation of beliefs and communication on cellular sheaves

The follow-up lets a chosen set of restriction maps adapt along with the opinions, and gives a condition that rules out agreement by collapse, where opinions drain to zero or the communication maps become trivial. It names evolving stalks, agents whose opinion spaces themselves change, as an open problem. We read the abstract, introduction, conclusion and the theorem statements, not the proofs.

What the paper says: Biesel, McSwiggen, Theodosopoulos and Titelbaum (2025), Topological obstructions to shared priors

This is the gluing question of Section 1.2 for beliefs. Each agent holds a probability measure on the part of the state space she is aware of, and the question is whether one measure on the whole space lies behind all of them. For agents who are pairwise compatible, the log ratio of two agents’ probabilities of a common event is a one-cocycle, and the paper’s Theorem 4.1 says it is a coboundary exactly when such a common prior exists. Theorem 4.2 says that pairwise checks suffice for every configuration of agents if and only if the overlap complex has no first cohomology, that is, no holes. That is a precise form of the sentence about trees and loops. Their Example 2.6 shows that adding a fourth agent who fills a hole can make pairwise compatibility impossible. We read pages 1 to 8 in full and the statements of the two theorems, not the cohomology background in Section 3 or the proofs.

What the paper says: Abramsky and Brandenburger (2011), The sheaf-theoretic structure of non-locality and contextuality

The paper does for probability tables what this chapter did for heights. A measurement is a question, a context is a set of questions that can be asked together, and an empirical model is one probability distribution per context, agreeing wherever contexts overlap. A global section is one joint distribution behind all of them. The point we take from it for later is that over the real numbers, allowing negative weights, compatible families always glue, so that the entire obstruction in the probabilistic setting is non-negativity (Theorems 5.5 and 5.9). Chapter 9 uses this. We read the introduction and postlude in full, Sections 2 and 3 selectively and the statement of every main theorem; we did not read the proofs, the Kochen–Specker section or most of Section 9.

What the paper says: Kakade, Kearns and Ortiz (2004), Graphical economics

An exchange economy on a graph: each consumer may buy only from neighbors, and the price of a good can differ from node to node. They prove an equilibrium exists. Everyone has the same commodity space Rk, prices attach to sellers and not to pairs, and there are no translation maps, so this is the equilibrium machinery without frames. Their polynomial-time algorithm works for trees, and for graphs with loops they offer only a heuristic. That is the same dividing line as Section 1.3, met from the computational side. We read it in full except the algorithm’s internals.

What the paper says: Devereaux and Koppl (2024), The use of knowledge in open-ended systems

Economists. Every person at every date holds a private world, a theory and a set of primitive terms, and the paper’s results include that these differ across people and dates, that common knowledge is generally impossible, that people can agree to disagree, and that no observer inside the system can hold a complete and correct model of it. The formal engine is Gödel incompleteness applied to each person’s theory. The paper covers the three objections of the first book, and with Hayek behind it, it is where the project’s starting point should be credited. The paper has no formal structure relating one person’s world to another’s: no overlaps, no translation maps, no measure of how far worlds are from fitting. It does name what connects them, institutions such as markets and law that people adopt because shared knowledge is not free, and niches of people who interact more and share more, but it leaves how these work outside its scope. The sheaf starts where it stops. We read Sections 1 to 5 in full. Of the appendix we read the statements of the definitions and results, not the proofs. Its central claim that different people’s worlds are disjoint in a technical sense is stated as a conjecture with a proof sketch.

What the paper says: Jiang, Lim, Yao and Ye (2011), Statistical ranking and combinatorial Hodge theory

Pairwise comparisons are an edge flow on a graph. The paper splits it orthogonally into a gradient part, the best global ranking in least squares, and a cyclic part, which measures how far the ranking can be trusted, and splits the cyclic part again into a curl part, inconsistency on triangles, and a harmonic part, inconsistency only on longer loops. In our language this is imδ and its orthogonal complement, with a finer cut of the second. It is this chapter’s last two sections for the constant sheaf. The paper says that cyclic inconsistency may be an inherent feature of the data, citing Condorcet, and gives no sampling distribution or test for it; its reliability measures are descriptive. We read the introduction and the statement of every definition, lemma and theorem in the arXiv version, and did not read the proofs, Section 3 or most of Sections 4 and 7.

1.7What we found

This chapter covers no research cycle by itself. It covers the ground the cycles stand on, and the checks we ran on that ground before running anything else. There are three findings, and one of them reversed.

The sheaf notes and two literature checks

The first thing we wrote was a short set of notes defining a sheaf on a network and working three examples, then asking what would make this more than a new vocabulary for old results. The notes made three conjectures and we checked them on November 10, 2026. The first check was about ten web searches and a reading of passages of one paper. The second was eight searches, which turned up five papers read at the level of abstracts.

Hansen and Ghrist had written the notes’ core. After the first check the notes’ account of sheaves on a network, the Laplacian and the diffusion to H0 was identified as their work. The first conjecture, that closing a loop can destroy the agreement a population can hold, which the notes had called the most distinctive because it runs against the presumption that more communication helps, turned out to be elementary. H0 is cut out by one linear condition per edge, so adding an edge adds a condition and cannot enlarge H0. The notes record a known version for signed networks, from Altafini (2013), which the searches found and we have not read. The lab notebook later lists the headline “adding links destroys agreement” as trivial and dropped. The other two conjectures fared no better: the second corresponds to what that literature calls frustration, and the third, that settling time is governed by the smallest positive eigenvalue of the Laplacian, is Hansen and Ghrist’s own result. All three were already known as mathematics within the day.

The full read of Hansen and Ghrist overturned a second claim. The first check had read only passages of Sections 4, 6 and 12. The notes had described the analyst placed inside the model, as one more node whose data pass through restriction maps, as a restatement of the identification problem, and had left open whether it yields anything new. Theorem 9 of the full paper states that identification condition, though without proof. The same read found a model of how frames change to fit views (Theorem 11), which the notes had called probably the hardest of the three objections. Both are theirs, and neither carries an economic reading in the paper. The first check’s description of what was left was therefore too generous to the project.

The gap, as it stood after both checks. The mathematics of views, frames, adjustment and obstruction exists, and three of the papers found had appeared in the previous twelve months, so the gap was closing. The searches did not find an exchange economy in which agents hold different commodity or state spaces joined by translation maps, with preferences, an equilibrium notion and a statement of when one price system fails to exist. Graphical economics has the equilibrium without the frames and the sheaf literature has the frames without the economics. They also did not find an empirical loop-consistency measure for economic data other than currency cross rates. Finding nothing means only that these searches found nothing.

Cycle 1: what a tree can and cannot tell you

The first research cycle turned the loop sum into a statistical test on ten nodes with noise of standard deviation 0.05, and Chapter 3 gives the test. The structural part belongs here, because it confirms Section 1.3 and Table 1.1 by experiment.

Ten nodes Edges Loops Redundancy Edge named
E−V+1 per edge (shift 0.5)
Path 9 0 0 undefined
Ring 10 1 0.10 0.092 (chance 0.10)
Ring plus 5 chords 15 6 0.39–0.42 0.998 (chance 0.067)
Complete 45 36 0.80 1.000

The loop counts are exactly E−V+1, and the redundancy per edge, the diagonal of the residual projector, averages the number of loops over the number of edges: 1/10, 6/15, 36/45. On the ring and the complete graph every edge gets exactly that share; with chords it ranges from 0.39 to 0.42. On the path the residual projector is zero to rounding error, with diagonal entries between −8.9×10−16 and 2.2×10−16, so nothing a tree reports can be tested. On the ring a shift of 0.2 on one edge is detected about a quarter of the time (0.247, against a size of 0.058), and a shift of 0.5 cannot be located: the hit rate for naming the shifted edge, 0.092, is chance. An edge has to lie on several loops before the loop sums can point at it.

Two limits on this finding. The red-team step found that geodesy already has it: Baarda’s reliability theory gives each observation a redundancy number, and a tree is the case in which every number is zero. We read that literature as a search summary only, and the searches did not return a source that states the zero-redundancy case outright, so that attribution still has to be verified in a geodesy text. And Abramsky (2013), which we read in full later, contains a far more general statement: on an acyclic cover, compatible tables always glue, for sets and for probabilities alike (Vorob’ev, 1962), so every test of coherence lives on the cycles. Chapter 9 takes that up. The experiment found a special case of an older theorem.

A check on the numbers in this chapter

Table 1.1 was computed from matrices, not from the formula, and the constant-sheaf rows agree with c and E−V+c on all five. The foot of the perpendicular in Figure 1.5 came from least squares and matches the closed form, the report minus a third of its loop sum. The hill’s lists were rounded to the centimeter before differencing, and the script asserts that the two reports of B to D agree and that the offset between the lists equals the true height of C above A.

Try it

Try it 1.1. Next market day the reports on the triangle are tAB=0.50, tBC=−0.20, tCA=−0.30. Could there be heights behind them? If yes, find some. You will have a choice to make. What is it, in terms of H0 of the constant sheaf, and why does it not matter?

Try it 1.2. For the constant sheaf on a square with one diagonal, compute dim⁡H0 and dim⁡H1 and write down two independent loop sums. Table 1.1 gives the answer; find it without the table, from a spanning tree, and check that your two loops are independent.

Try it 1.3. Add a hamlet E that tracks only wheat and trades with both A and B in the three-town example. Write the two new rows of the matrix δ, in the order (wA,fA,wB,cB,fC,cC,wE). Which loop has appeared, in which good? What are dim⁡H0 and dim⁡H1 now, and which row of Table 1.1 should you get?

Try it 1.4. Cover a circle by two arcs whose overlap consists of two separate pieces, one at each end. Let two local potentials have the same slope on the overlap, with offsets c on one piece and c′ on the other. The graph of overlaps has two vertices and two edges. Show that the two potentials can be shifted into one if and only if c=c′, and say which loop sum that is. Apply it to the angle around the circle: on each arc the angle is a potential, and the two potentials differ by 0 on one overlap piece and by a full turn on the other. What does your result say?

Try it 1.5. In Figure 1.3, load the chapter example and read the loop sum, the least-squares heights and the misclosure. Press “Replace by closest consistent reports” and watch the misclosure vanish. Then choose a report under “cut the ring at” and watch the loop sum stop mattering. Do the heights depend on which report you cut? Say why, in terms of what the discarded report was telling you.
